p:
Thank you, uh, Council Member. I think, um, so, uh, approximately 620 events last year, uh, reaching, uh, 75,000 New Yorkers. Um, I think the breakdown is kind of half and half between consumer protection and worker protection. Uh, it's, it's a, it's a team, small team, 5 people. I like to think they're the best outreach team in the city though, because they burn a lot of shoe leather. Um, our model is to really plug into community-based organizations and their ongoing meetings, membership meetings. Whenever you have a meeting, we are gonna be there to go, um, uh, as a way to get out there and to

every— be, be broad and deep with our outreach. Um, with respect to deep theft, you know, I— we coordinate closely with the Department of Aging, for example, on their booklets, um, that provide educational resources and, and referrals over to our financial empowerment centers. We also coordinate closely with HPD's homeowner help desk as well, which really helps address a lot of these, the theft issues too. Um, and in the, the home improvement contractor space, you know, I think we have done a lot of work over the past few years, and I can maybe toss it over to Mike about this, um, revitalizing how we, uh, disburse restitution through our trust funds and other enforcement work.

Yeah, we- we have a, uh, home improvement contractor trust fund that, as, uh, Carlos mentioned, we've revamped the sort of, uh, operating rules under. So now that, uh, you can— we have a more streamlined process where you can get up to $20,000 in relief without having to file a case. And we also increased the cap if you do file a case in civil court, how much you can, uh, get from the trust fund.

We also have a home improvement contractor wall of shame on our website. Um, that's for repeat violators of unlicensed home improvement contracting. It's very important for consumers, and we make— that's something, an educational point we really try to get out to consumers, that they should check our website which has a license lookup function to see if their home— the home improvement contractor they're considering hiring is licensed by us, because you get a lot more protections under the law if you hire a licensed home improvement contractor. And so if you go to our website, you'll see the most recent bad actors as far as unlicensed home improvement contracting, just sort of responding to your question, Council Member, of, like, where are the bad actors? That's at least one, um, sliver of the pie where we actually do have something on our website.
Thank you.
Thank you and I— we're also joined by Council Member Banks on Zoom. I want to turn it over to Council Member Abreu.

Thank you, Chair. My question is, Commissioner, does the Mayor's Office of

Management and Budget still have a 2-in-1 out-of-hiring requirement implemented for DCWP's hiring policies?
Uh, at the moment, yes, Council Member.
Huh. Um, I, so this is not— I thought they were supposed to be all gone. What happened? Why this is not— why isn't the DCW being— why are you being subject to this?

Well, we have— we got, uh, savings targets by OMB. Um, um, we're in discussions with OMB about those cuts. My understanding is if and when that's— when that is resolved, uh, the 2-for-1 will be lifted. But Carlos, do you want to add more details on that process?
No, that's, that's 100% correct, Commissioner. We, um, we have— we're under 2-for-1 until we identified our savings targets.

I, I mean, I'm shocked to hear that your agency is being subject to the 2-to-1, and I'll tell you why. Uh, you know, the Council's done— obviously passed legislation that you're going to be tasked with enforcing. Uh, for instance, um, I passed a package of bills on, on tipping

transparency, pay transparency, something I've worked very closely with WJP on. Um, how do you— I would imagine you need more resources to implement these laws, is that correct? Or do you think you have the headcount necessary to implement those laws?

No, it is true, Council Member, that OMB identified the needs for your legislation and others, uh, with respect to how we can effectively implement these laws, and there are significant additional needs. I can go through them if that's helpful.

I mean, in addition to that, the Council also passed a slew of bills led by the Street Vendor Project to expand licensing for street vendors. We expect those licenses to be out the door as soon as the law requires, and it sounds like this hiring policy— this 2-for-1 hiring policy is severely limiting your ability to do your job. What is the— what is the ask that we need to make from this Administration to help you do your job between now and exec?

Well, we're committed to full, robust implementation of the street vendor license expansion. I was proud to— our Administration

reversed the previous Administration's opposition to that bill. We were happy to see the Council override the veto. But it is the case, as you alluded to, that, uh, the fiscal impact statement for the license expansion identified 26 new lines uh, that DCWP would need to implement it effectively. Um, we are— we are having ongoing conversations with OMB, with City Hall about how, uh, those needs might be reflected in the exec plan. But, you know, whatever happens, we are committed to making this a success.
It's not whatever happens. We need the resources and so our job is to make sure that you have those resources. I like to know how much money you need to do it.
Well, the fiscal impact statement put forward with the legislation identified 26 lines, $3.1 million in FY '27, $2.5 million in out years.
How many worker rights and consumer rights attorneys—
Just to clarify, that's for just that one bill?
That is just for street vendor licenses.
That's 26 for just for street vendors, not to mention everything else what we did, right?
Correct.
So what is the overall— can I use that?
Yeah, please.
What is the overall increase in staffing that you would need according to OMB to cover all the laws that we've passed?
If, if you include the laws that were passed in 27— what year is it? 26.
Yes.
Um, 302 new lines um, and, uh, I can give you the breakdown of, hmm, but 302 new lines s.
That's— Chair, I think these, these, uh, these fiscal impacts are available on, uh, City Legistar, so we're happy to forward you over the
Is it your position that you- you have to enforce these laws?
Absolutely.
And is it also your position that you need the resources necessary to enforce these laws?
Yes. And - but, but I also want to be clear, we recognize the city's in a budget crisis. Whatever our— the allocation is, we're going to do our best to enforce these laws effectively.

I think we need DCWP to get it— the resources that you need. I know that you can't— I know there's some limitations on what you can say here today. I have no limitations. I can say whatever I want. Sort of like Gail. Nah, I'm just kidding. Um, Gail always says what she wants. But seriously, we need to get you the resources that you need and we need to get all those lines that- that you need to do your job. The advocates in this room from WJP to DRUM to the Laundry Workers Center, to WJP, I think I already said that, and everyone else, like, we, we are committed, uh, to this issue and again, we want you to do your jobs. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member.
You catch her like that.

No, I just, I just, I think I, I want to add, like, I think we would need a breakdown of where the need is for increased headcount, like how many lawyers do you need? How many, you know, education folks, you know, on the ground do you need? Because I, I think I, I, and again, I'm going to emphasize how important it is for, you know, workers and consumers, small businesses to be educated on what their rights are, where they can go, uh, to make a complaint, uh, what resources are available to them. And because they're just— folks are not gonna— the law is not going to be enforced if people don't know- know about it and, um, so I would like to hear more about how much do you need, you know, uh, on the education side as well, um, to, uh, to have a fully functioning agency that's gonna be able to do, do its work appropriately?

Well, we appreciate that, Council Member. Um, certainly with respect to the laws that were passed, there are publicly available fiscal impact statements. I'll give you a couple of the highlights. For-hire vehicle delivery deactivation was estimated to require 170 lines, delivery worker deactivation 34 lines, street vendor license

expansion 26 lines, delivery worker expansion 14 lines, and, and on and on. Um, I believe that these estimates do include the resources necessary to do outreach around these laws. Um, but it is also the case that since these laws were passed, um, the Mayor has issued significant executive orders, uh, charging DCWP, for example, with leading a citywide— all of— whole of government crackdown on junk fees, directing DCWP to lead a crackdown on subscription traps, directing DCWP to co-organize the rent-a-ripoff hearings. We're excited about this. We've never had a Mayor, in my opinion, as relentlessly as committed to consumer and worker protection but the needs for our agency continue to grow. Um, and that is reflected in, um, um, I think all of our testimony today.
Thank, thank you. Uh, uh, Council Member Krishnan.

Thanks so much, Chair Epstein. Good to see you Commissioner, First Deputy Commissioner, and team, as always, and appreciate your work and our conversation so far about all we can do together for protecting all of our workers and small businesses and drivers.

I wanted to follow a couple questions. Some of them kind of follow up on, on the conversation we were just having, which is, um, as you well know, separate and apart from the street vendor package, we passed historic legislation to protect, uh, Uber and Lyft drivers in the city, overrode the Mayor's veto, uh, to do that. And, you know, this has been the biggest issue facing drivers in the city since the medallion crisis. But the biggest question now is going to be ensuring and I know we've had conversations about this and appreciate your partnership and you mentioning in your opening statement too. Um, I would love to get a better sense of what are the resources you all need, um, from a dollar standpoint? I know you just briefly touched on it, but if you can give a little bit more detail about what are the resources you need from a dollar standpoint, um, to implement this, um, from a staffing standpoint, what kind of staffing are we talking about? Um, and what is the plan, uh, currently, um, to, to, you know, separate from the staffing needs, how are we gonna start working together to implement it? And I know you all share

the same goal that we do on it, so it's just a question of making it happen together.

Well, I think, Council Member, let me just start by saying the— how critical this legislation is, which is why we supported it. I have spoken to, and I know you have too, uh, Uber drivers, or, you know, I don't remember specifically Uber, but rideshare drivers who wake up one day and they can't log in. They've been deact— now, deactivation is sort of a technical term, but it means they lose their livelihood. They don't know why. They had no due process. There's nowhere really to go, no one to call, uh, they don't know what to do and then there are downstream consequences. Maybe they're being peddled out predatory lending products. Maybe now, uh, you know, they're being affected by scams. Um, so this is a major crisis facing thousands of workers throughout our city and the laws that the Council passed around delivery worker deactivation and a for-hire vehicle are not only a necessary corrective, but in my opinion, a national and international model. Um, that said, they do require significant resources according to analysis, uhm because we are

anticipating a significant volume of complaints. As you know, there's a look-back period, so within the first year, I believe anybody who's been deactivated 6 years prior— so we're expecting a flood of complaints from, from the jump. Um, what OMB has estimated, uh, is that a for-hire vehicle would require 400— excuse me, 170 lines. 4.2 million in FY '27, 23 million in out years. Uh, delivery worker deactivation, 34 lines, 1.3 million in '27, 5 million in out years. And Liz, if you'd like to weigh in sort of how we're thinking about implementation, with the caveat that this is gonna be very resource dependent.

Yeah, I would just, um, add that, you know, we are already looking at, you know, rulemaking and some of the sort of internal work that, um, would be needed to make these protections real. But, um, you know, without resources, we're unable to do things like, um, create the complaint interface on our online complaint filing portal, um, you know, have systems to track how many cases are coming in, and then obviously investigators and attorneys to take the cases, talk to workers, interview them, investigate, uh, what's the real

reason for their deactivation, what's the evidence, did the company do an independent investigation to um, into the circumstances that led to the deactivation. Was it an algorithm or a person who made the final decision? All of these core protections that the law creates, um, you know, we obviously need, um, people to be able to, to, to handle all of those, um, cases for workers.

And I, you know, I think that's something we should give— I mean, of course, first and foremost is going to be the funding piece and making sure that we have that in place. And, you know, you have our full commitment here in the Council to, to work with you all to ensure that. Um, I know it's obviously a top priority for- for City Hall and our Mayor too. Um, but, you know, but I think that's where the rubber really meets the road, is to make sure we get those resources in place. Um, what I, I look forward to is working with all to do so. I know your commitment. You've got a great team here, a great First Deputy Commissioner that, uh, as a constituent as well, and worked very hard on this issue with me for a very long time. So I know the- the will is

there. Um, and let's, let's figure out how we can, we can make that happen. It would be great to have, as Council Member Aldebol mentioned too, just a breakdown of these different programs that we've passed that are priorities for both of our— both of us, you know, what, what the needs are specifically. How have the conversations been with City Hall, uh, on that front in terms of making sure that, you know, we— as we move to executive budget, these programs get the funding that we need?

I think the Mayor has made very clear that this is a significant priority for him. I mean, since his time in the Assembly, of course, he stood with us when we returned $5 million to, uh, underpaid deliveryistas, um, and also got 10,000 workers actually react— er, ah, hmm, eligible for reactivation. Um, in terms of the budget, you know, those conversations are ongoing, but, you know, it is certainly a matter of public record that I think the city is aware of that there are significant needs that have been identified for successful implementation of these laws. Uh, but those conversations are ongoing.

Great, good to hear. And then look forward to- to more data on that and more conversations. On another note, um, you know, shifting more to the immigration context, um, a big issue that we are seeing in neighborhoods like mine in Jackson Heights, on Roosevelt Avenue and around there too, um, are a lot of individuals who are in desperate need of help, but, you know, notarios or others engaging in immigration fraud, um, which, uh, is happening more and more, and I'm hearing more about it too. What, what are the number of complaints that DCWP has received on that issue? Um, how have you all taken action and what are your plans going forward to, to, to help address it?

Oh, thank, thank you, Council Member. We just want— we just want to make sure we get you the right numbers here. Um, so with respect to— let me just start by saying, for as long as I've been in consumer protection, immigrants face— and I know everyone here knows this— unique vulnerabilities. And this year it is worse than I have ever seen, worse than our allies on the ground have ever seen. Given many people- many immigrants

feel they can't report scams to government. Many companies unfortunately feel emboldened to rip off their workers because they can threaten workers with retaliation through ICE or otherwise. One of the things we are hammering over and over every meeting any of us does is if, if you wanna file a complaint with us, go, go through your— go through Make the Road, go through, uh, New York Immigrant Coalition, whatever it is. You don't— if you don't wanna give your name to us, that's fine. Go through a group. We'll hand— we'll take in the complaint. We'll reach out. We'll do the investigation. We want people to be able to file complaints without fear of retaliation. Um, with respect to the number of complaints, uh, we had 30 complaints in 2025 compared to 46 the previous year around immigration services providers. Um, and what we're seeing is that a lot of these scams are moving online, which makes year-over-year comparisons quite challenging. I don't know if either of you wanna add anything to that?

No, of course, this has been a priority for several years for us. I mean, I can say that every single complaint, uh, coming from an

immigrant goes to the highest levels of, uh, our consumer protection enforcement attorneys, and we look at each one individually. To reinforce what the Commissioner says, uh, we— you can submit complaints anonymously, you can submit it through an advocate, we— whatever makes sense for an immigrant to be able to get information for us. We wanna make that happen and so we can talk to 'em. We actually have a case currently pending at OATH, the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, against a notario who has, uh, repeatedly been preying on the Ecuadorian community in Queens.
Mhm hmm.

So this is something that we do face significant systemic challenges given where we are in 2026, but something that we are very dedicated to continue to work on and try to find the best solutions. And when we get immigrants who are willing to talk to us, we will take action.
I would appreciate that.

I would add to Council Member, to your point about what we're doing. Uh, we're also, uh, er, in the midst of, uh, citywide sweeps of

immigrant— of notarios, fraudulent, fraudulent immigration service providers. Um, we've also dedicated some OTPs as well to digital advertising to try and meet these consumers where they are, to the Commissioner's point about a lot of this stuff moving on digital. And we also plan to be, uh, starting up some in-person outreach as well, uh, in April leading into July.

Just, and just one, uh, final point for the entire Committee, um, like, we have two buckets of laws that we can actually enforce. We have the consumer protection law, which applies to all businesses, no matter the subject, but we have very specific laws that this Council has passed for immigration service providers and we supported a bill last year that actually increased the penalties, um, for violations of the immigration services provider law. We have a lot of great materials online uh, for Immigrant Bill of Rights, um, that can give information to all immigrants. And I know, uh, Carlos's team has, like, they're out on the field spreading the word about that. So I just wanted to sort of just make sure everyone knows what the tools are in our arsenal.

I appreciate that and I would just say, you know, in closing, I think, you know, I think two, two things are on my mind. One is, um, I think, Commissioner, you, you're right to point out that a lot of this is shifting towards digital you know, fraudulent, uh, services being advertised online. So DCWP figuring out ways to be more present digitally on social media to do so. The other issue, obviously, and you all know well too, you know, we just had a hearing in, in, in my Oversight Committee about, uh, the sanctuary laws and the city's compliance with them. One of the main things that I hit on there too was when the sanctuary laws aren't complied with, they make immigrants feel afraid to come forward to government for any kinds of services. And so maybe one thing we can think about too is partnering together in Jackson Heights, you know, and then Queens, um, to do, uh, events so that you are out there in the neighborhoods with us, letting people know that you're there to assist, to combat, um, immigration fraud, um, and other kind of, you know, uh, fraudulent behavior that we're seeing that could, you know, um, exploit, uh, vulnerable

communities in this moment right now. And that might be a way, uh, to make sure that what DCWP is doing, those efforts get out there more too.
We- we are deeply committed to this work and we'd be very happy to partner with you on that, so.
Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member. Um, so I just wonder if maybe that breakdown is really going to be helpful for us. Um, you know, I know Council Member Abreu talked about, um, the- the, ah, the- the laws we passed around protecting people's work weeks. What do you feel like you have enough staffing right now to cover the needs that are out there and the complaints you're getting, or do you need— do you, as OMB say, you need additional lines there?

Well, there is a backlog right now, Chair, uh, around our worker protection cases. It is a 6-month backlog. And what that means is that— and, and this is certainly not for inefficiency. We— I, again, I've, I've worked at a number of law enforcement agencies. This is the

leanest, meanest team I have worked with. Um, but the fact of the matter is the case— you know, we are very proud when we can go out and announce, say, $5 million back for workers, whether it's fair work week, or the $38 million for Starbucks workers on Fair Work Week, or $5 million for minimum pay. But many times these are workers whose— where the violations occurred years earlier, where companies have been sitting on their money for years, and we're just getting work. And for- for low-income, middle, even middle-income workers, they can't afford to be underpaid and then get a check 2 or 3 years later. So I don't know if, Liz, if you want to add any additional topics to that.
Can I just say, on the 6-month backlog, you mean from beginning to, to review the case.
Liz, do you wanna describe the—

Yeah, that's exac— that's exactly right. So from the date the worker files a complaint to when, um, we have an investigator available to start investigating it, it's currently 6 months and that's just a huge explosion in complaint volumes that began in Fiscal 2024, but, um, really

accelerated in January of this year with the passage of the new laws and new laws going into effect uhm.
I would, I would just clarify one point. The- the workers receive communications immediately from the agency, and then that communication outlines to them their expectation of, of wait time.

Yeah, and I appreciate that they're getting communication, but if you're a low-wage worker and you're waiting 6 months until the investigation begins, I mean, you may not even have that job anymore. You- you know, people who are in deep economic straits may not even live in that same place anymore and so, if it takes 6 months to begin the complaint, then you need to investigate the complaint. And I'm sure— I don't know how many— what's your average timeline to— for just those complaints? I assume it's a few months, right?

Um, yeah, especially when the— our most impactful cases, um, you know, can take some time, right? Because once we do the interview of the worker, um, and we learn that it's a systemic issue that affects a lot of people, um, you know, those are our highest-dollar cases in the end, um,

but do take usually about a year on average to, to complete. Um, so it, you know, it, it is something that we deeply worry about internally, um, and obviously want to move those cases forward more quickly.
And I assume that with additional staffing, that backlog will go away, am I right?
Yes.

All right, so right now we're talking to people who are at workplace violations, they're going to wait potentially a year and a half to 2 years before they can see some redress, especially on the larger cases. The population— there's a lot of turnover in low-wage worker, you know, once you're working at McDonald's and there's turnover. So even finding those people a year and a half later might be really difficult. Is that correct?

Um, it could be, you know, we- we do have very good systems for finding all workers or finding as many as possible. It's our practice in our workplace wide cases to get an employee contact list from the company, um, and send

text messages and emails to all workers who worked at the business to gather information about violations.
Right.
Um, but obviously our— we, we expect that our response rates would be higher with, with a fresher list.

And what is your current response rate when you send them? Obviously we all get text messages and emails from people we think is fraud. We talked about all these scams a few minutes ago. How do they know it's actually coming from you versus some, you know, hey, you're entitled to money, you know, call us. I mean, most people probably don't respond to that, you know.

You know, we- we get much better response rates than we used to get when we would just call a phone list. People actually do seem to enjoy, you know, text messaging with our investigators and filling out the survey that we send. Um, um, so, you know, we feel good about our system reaching more people than ever before.
So what is your response rate for kind of these larger cases?
Oh, it varies by case, it can be 10%, it can be 30%.
Is it— so is that on average between 10% and 30% response rate?
That's, that's quite rough. You know, I didn't pull the numbers before this hearing. It's anecdotal, but it's about what— that's about what it is.
So the majority of workers are not getting back to you?
I would say that we feel good about those response rates, really. Um, it- it does give us a very clear sense of what's going on in a business and a workplace-wide case.
Yeah, I appreciate that, but if we're talking about a 10 to 30% response rate, that means either 90 or 70% of people are not responding, right?
That's true. A lot of people don't wanna say anything negative about an employer.
Yeah, or maybe they don't know it's you and they can't prove it's you, so they— like, we ignore some things because we don't know what it is, you know?
It could be.
Yeah.

But, Chair, if I might add, and Liz, correct me if I'm wrong, that is in terms of the response rate to shape the- the scope of the investigation. At the end of the day, if we find workplace-wide investigations, we would still aim to distribute redress to 100% of the affected workers.
That's right, everyone gets money.
And how do you find everyone if they don't respond to you?

We have, um, a lot of different ways of doing that. Um, so at the end of a case, we'll get from a company, um, an address list and an updated, um, email and phone list. Uhm, we then usually may— it's usually by mail that the checks go out, um, although in some cases we'll do direct deposit if we have the bank information from the employer. Um, we then, um, have systems for, um, any checks that aren't cashed or deposits— or rather deposited, um, to call everyone who didn't deposit their check, um, to email everyone who didn't deposit their check.

Um, and although I don't have sort of check deposit numbers here, percentages, they're very high. Um, um, they're, they're very high. We get most money to people who are owed money.
Thank you. According to OMB, for the delivery workers law expansion, what addition— how many additional lines do you think you need?
For the -
For 1135 delivery workers?
Yeah, I just want to confirm. Yeah, I know, but I want to go ahead, Carlos.
I was gonna say, I think, um, it was, uh, it was 23 lines, and I think we received 9 lines in the Preliminary Budget.
Okay, so you needed 23, you got 9, so you're 14 short.
It's a— there's a 34.
Did you say delivery worker expansion or delivery worker deactivation?
Worker expansion?
Oh, oh.
Yes, so now we're at 14.
And how about deactivation?
So delivery worker deactivation is 34. For-hire vehicle deactivation is 170.
That's what you need or that's what you're short?
Well-
According to OMB, what do they think?
That was the estimated need.
That was our initial estimate.
Compared to what you got, how many did you get?
Oh, wait, that's still in the process of this Executive Budget turn.
So you have none right now?
That's correct.
And so they said 34, OMB said 34?

OMB said 34, but I- I do just want to note that the Preliminary Budget, as I understand, was based on new laws that were passed in '26. The deactivation laws were passed, of course, in '27 by an override. So those we expect would be— those needs we expect would be reflected in the exec.
And just for the for-hire, uh, Uber, Lyft, uh, expansion, what do you think— what's OMB think that additional lines you might need?
So 170 lines that are currently not budgeted for, right?
Correct.

Correct, similarly, as the Commissioner mentioned, you know, those went through a veto. The Council thankfully overrode that veto, and now we've submitted, um, those needs, uh, for the Executive Budget.
And, um, how about the security guard minimum wage? Kind of where do you have— according to OMB, have sufficient staffing there?
Uh, the- the- the fiscal impact statement for that bill identified a need of 41 lines.
41 additional lines that you don't have right now.
That’s correct.

I know Council Member Krishnan talked about the immigration service providers and kind of the fraud going on there. Um, is— can we determine if they needed- according to OMB, need additional lines there?
What was identified was one additional line.
That's OMB's identification.
Yes.
And, uh, licensing for self-storage warehouse. I know you brought some self-storage litigation earlier this year.

That's exactly right, though that was of course under our consumer protection law rather than licensing. In terms of the licensing, uh, 6 additional lines, and there's also some OTPS for the IT back office.
And that street vendor expansion, what do you think you might need for additional lines there as well?
Well, that's significant. That's, uh, 26 lines.
Okay, so that's how we got to your number earlier, the 300—
Correct.
—Odd lines that you need.
